title: Astrological sign
description: Twelve 30° sectors of the ecliptic, as defined by Western astrology
wiki_lead:
In Western astrology, astrological signs are the zodiac, twelve 30-degree sectors that are crossed by the Sun's 360-degree orbital path as viewed from Earth in its sky. The signs enumerate from the first day of spring, known as the First Point of Aries, which is the vernal equinox. The astrological signs are Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. The Western zodiac originated in Babylonian astrology, and was later influenced by the Hellenistic culture. Each sign was named after a constellation the sun annually moved through while crossing the sky. This observation is emphasized in the simplified and popular sun sign astrology. Over the centuries, Western astrology's zodiacal divisions have shifted out of alignment with the constellations they were named after by axial precession of the Earth while Hindu astrology measurements correct for this shifting. Astrology (i.e. a system of omina based on celestial appearances) was developed in Chinese and Tibetan cultures as well but these astrologies are not based upon the zodiac but deal with the whole sky.
Astrology is a pseudoscience. Scientific investigations of the theoretical basis and experimental verification of claims have shown it to have no scientific validity or explanatory power. More plausible explanations for the apparent correlation between personality traits and birth months exist, such as the influence of seasonal birth in humans.
According to astrology, celestial phenomena relate to human activity on the principle of "as above, so below", so that the signs are held to represent characteristic modes of expression. Scientific astronomy used the same sectors of the ecliptic as Western astrology until the 19th century.
Various approaches to measuring and dividing the sky are currently used by differing systems of astrology, although the tradition of the Zodiac's names and symbols remain mostly consistent. Western astrology measures from Equinox and Solstice points (points relating to equal, longest, and shortest days of the tropical year), while Hindu astrology measures along the equatorial plane (sidereal year).

Western zodiac signs


History

Western astrology is a direct continuation of Hellenistic astrology as recorded in Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos in the 2nd century. Hellenistic astrology in turn was partly based on concepts from Babylonian tradition. Specifically, the division of the ecliptic in twelve equal sectors is a Babylonian conceptual construction. This division of the ecliptic originated in the Babylonian "ideal calendar" found in the old compendium MUL.APIN and its combination with the Babylonian lunar calendar, represented as the "path of the moon" in MUL.APIN. In a way, the zodiac is the idealisation of an ideal lunar calendar.

grok_lead: An astrological sign, also known as a zodiac sign, is one of the twelve equal divisions of the zodiac, a conceptual belt encircling the Earth along the ecliptic âthe apparent path of the Sun across the skyâeach spanning 30 degrees and associated with specific constellations, personality traits, and symbolic meanings in astrology. Astrology, including the interpretation of these signs, is considered a pseudoscience by the scientific community. The twelve signs, in order, are Aries (the Ram), Taurus (the Bull), Gemini (the Twins), Cancer (the Crab), Leo (the Lion), Virgo (the Maiden), Libra (the Scales), Scorpio (the Scorpion), Sagittarius (the Archer), Capricorn (the Sea-Goat), Aquarius (the Water Bearer), and Pisces (the Fish), with dates approximately from March 21 to April 19 for Aries through February 19 to March 20 for Pisces in the tropical zodiac system used in Western astrology. These signs form the basis for horoscopes and natal charts, where the position of the Sun (and other planets) at an individual's birth time is believed to influence their character and destiny. The origins of astrological signs trace back to ancient Mesopotamia, particularly Babylonian astronomy in the second millennium BCE, where priests divided the sky into twelve constellations for omen interpretation and celestial tracking, as documented in cuneiform texts like the Enuma Anu Enlil series containing over 7,000 omens. In the 5th century BCE, the Babylonians formalized the zodiac into twelve equal 30-degree segments, naming them after animal and mythical figures such as "The Lion" for Leo. This system was later adopted and refined by ancient Greek astronomers and astrologers following Alexander the Great's conquests around 330 BCE, integrating Babylonian and Egyptian influences to create the zodiac as a "circle of animals" (zÅdiakos kyklos), with the signs aligned to the Sun's annual path. In the second century CE, the Alexandrian scholar Claudius Ptolemy codified the Western astrological framework in his influential text Tetrabiblos, establishing the tropical zodiacâfixed to the seasons via solstices and equinoxes rather than actual star positionsâand linking each sign to one of four classical elements (fire, earth, air, water) and three modalities (cardinal, fixed, mutable) to describe temperaments and influences. For instance, fire signs (Aries, Leo, Sagittarius) are associated with energy and initiative, while cardinal signs (Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricorn) initiate action. This structure spread through Roman, medieval European, and Islamic scholarship, evolving into modern Western astrology, though it differs from sidereal systems in Vedic or Chinese traditions that align more closely with current constellation positions.
